rows.verified: HSE's Management Standards provide a step-by-step risk-assessment approach for managing work-related stress.
Employers can assess the current situation using existing data, surveys and other evidence.
The approach promotes active discussion and partnership with employees and their representatives.
The Management Standards focus attention on underlying causes of work-related stress and prevention.
The six Management Standards areas are Demands, Control, Support, Relationships, Role and Change.
Demands include workload, work patterns and the work environment.
Organisations should provide adequate and achievable demands in relation to agreed working hours.
Organisations should make roles and responsibilities clear and provide a route for concerns about role conflict or uncertainty.
The appropriate controls depend on the organisation, job design, workforce, evidence and causes identified by the assessment.

rows.source: HSE stress and mental health at work
rows.verified: Work-related stress evidence is organisation- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level health probability.
Employers must protect workers from upper limb disorders caused or made worse by work.
Upper limb disorders can affect the shoulders, arms, wrists, hands, fingers and neck.
Employers should complete a suitable risk assessment for work that may cause upper limb disorders.
Prolonged repetitive work using the same hand or arm action is a recognised risk factor.

rows.source: HSE upper limb disorders in the workplace
rows.verified: Risk assessment should consider repetition, posture, force, exposure duration, environmental and psychosocial factors.
Employers should identify risks, control them and support workers who report symptoms.
Workers should be consulted and involved in identifying and reducing upper limb disorder risks.
Workers should know how to report symptoms or injuries early so that action can be taken.

rows.source: HSE upper limb disorders in the workplace
rows.verified: Risk depends on the actual task, posture, force, repetition, duration, recovery time and individual worker.
Upper-limb-disorder evidence is task- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury probability.
